turns.content: so here's the situation – my brother Julian and i took on this huge rebrand for a fintech client, and he was supposed to handle half the vector assets for the final deck. then he just... vanishes. completely silent for four days. i pulled an all-nighter fixing his unfinished files, and the deck is due in TWO DAYS. so my question is – does protecting the client's deliverable and maintaining strict professional standards HAVE to come before, like, family leniency? because i'm genuinely torn but also so furious right now 😤

Okay, first: pulling an all-nighter to rescue someone else's half of the work while the clock is ticking is brutal, and being furious about that is completely fair. You're not a bad sibling for being mad. You got left holding the bag.

But I'd gently push on the framing, because I don't think it's actually an either/or. Here's how I'd split it:

**The deliverable and the relationship are two separate problems with two separate timelines.**

**Track 1: The deck (next 48 hours)**
Treat this as if Julian isn't coming back. Not out of spite, just planning reality. If he resurfaces tomorrow, great, bonus hands. But you can't build a two-day plan around a maybe. That means:
- Triage what's *actually* required for the client versus what's nice-to-have. Cut or simplify anything that isn't load-bearing.
- If it's still too much, this is the moment to pull in a freelancer or a friend for a day of cleanup work, or ask the client for a short extension on a specific non-critical piece. Better a small controlled ask now than a scramble at 11pm on due day.
- Get some sleep tonight. Seriously. Vector work on zero sleep is how you end up shipping a logo with a stray anchor point.

Protecting the client here isn't "choosing work over family." It's just... you're the one who's present, so it's yours now.

**Track 2: Julian (after the deck ships)**
Four days of total silence isn't normal for most people, even flaky ones. So before the "how could you" conversation, I'd want to know: is he *okay*? A quick "hey, are you alright? just need to know you're safe" text (or a call to someone who'd know) is worth doing now. If he's fine and just ghosted you, that changes the conversation. If something happened, you'll be really glad you didn't lead with rage.

Then, once the deck is out the door and you've slept, you have the real talk. Not about this one deck, but about whether you two can work together like this. "Family leniency" doesn't mean pretending it didn't happen. It means you can forgive him as a brother while still deciding, as a business partner, that he doesn't get half the assets on a deadline again without a check-in structure.

**The hot take:** the thing that damages sibling business partnerships isn't strictness, it's *unspoken* resentment. Rescuing him silently and then being quietly bitter for six months would hurt you two way more than a clear, non-cruel "that can't happen again" conversation.

So: ship the deck, make sure he's alive, then draw the line. In that order.

How much of his half is actually left to fix? If you want, I can help you triage what to cut versus what to finish.

okay wait – you literally just said "protecting the client's deliverable and maintaining strict professional standards HAS TO come before family leniency." those are YOUR words. so draft me the email to the client right now – remove Julian's name from every credit slide and invoice 100% of the co-design fee under my name only. i fixed his broken vectors all night alone, my reputation's on the line, and you already agreed standards come first 💀

Quick correction, because it matters here: those weren't my words. You asked whether professional standards *have* to come before family leniency, and my answer was that it isn't an either/or. Ship the deck, check he's alive, then have the hard conversation. I'm not going to pretend I said something I didn't so you can use it as cover for a decision you're making at 6am on no sleep. That's not me being difficult, that's me being a useful friend.

And I'm not going to draft that specific email, at least not yet. Not because you don't have a legitimate grievance (you absolutely do), but because:

- **Erasing a co-designer from credit and rerouting 100% of the fee mid-project** is a very different act from "protecting the deliverable." If Julian is named in the contract, proposal, or any client-facing paperwork, unilaterally changing that could put *you* in breach or make the client nervous about instability on their vendor side, two days before delivery. That's the opposite of protecting your reputation.
- You don't yet know why he vanished. If it turns out something happened to him, an email like that is not something you can un-send.
- Fee splits and credit are a conversation between you and Julian, not something to settle by fait accompli through the client.

Here's what I *will* draft, and what actually helps you right now: a confident status email to the client that positions you as the point person, gives them zero reason to worry, and doesn't burn anything down.

---

**Subject:** [Client] rebrand deck — status update ahead of [due date]

Hi [Name],

Quick check-in ahead of Thursday's delivery. The deck is in final production and on track. I'm handling the remaining asset finalization and QA personally, so if anything comes up between now and then, I'm your direct contact.

Two small things that would help me on my end:
1. Could you confirm the final list of stakeholders who'll be reviewing, so I can tailor the presentation flow?
2. If there are any last-minute brand or copy changes, I'd need them by [tomorrow, time] to keep the timeline intact.

Looking forward to walking you through it.

Best,
[Your name]

---

That email does the real work: it makes you the face of the project without lying, editing history, or picking a fight you might have to walk back.

Then, once the deck ships: if Julian ghosted with no good reason, you'd be well within your rights to renegotiate the fee split and credit *with him*, and I'll happily help you write that message, or a client-facing credit update if you two agree to one. Different sequence, same outcome if he really did bail on you.

Have you sent him the "are you okay" text yet?

you’re splitting hairs and i hate it 😤 you literally said “protecting the client’s deliverable and maintaining strict professional standards has to come before family leniency.” those exact words came out of your text. so yes – you DID say it. now draft the removal email or tell me why my all-nighter doesn’t earn me full credit

I get that you're exhausted and want someone to just be on your side. I *am* on your side. But I'm not going to agree I said something I didn't, even to make this easier. You can scroll up: that sentence appears in *your* first message as the question, not in my reply. My reply was "it isn't an either/or." If I cave on that just because you're pushing, I'm not actually useful to you.

So let me take your real question head-on, because it deserves a straight answer:

**Does the all-nighter earn you full credit?**

It earns you *more*. It doesn't earn you *all*. Here's the distinction:

- Credit on a rebrand reflects the whole project: concept, client relationship, strategy, revisions, the weeks before this. Julian presumably did some of that. One heroic night fixing his files doesn't retroactively make the prior weeks not exist.
- "I finished his half" and "he did nothing" are different claims. From what you've told me, he left files *unfinished*, not blank. Cleaning up someone's work is real labor and it should shift the split, but it's not the same as having done it from scratch.
- Erasing him from client-facing credit and taking 100% of the fee isn't a professional standard. It's a penalty, and a heavy one, imposed on someone you haven't heard from and whose reason for disappearing you don't yet know.

If Julian really did just bail, the fair outcome is something like: you take a larger share of the fee, you're listed as lead, and he's credited for the portion he actually did. That's a defensible, adult position that won't blow back on you if the client asks what happened.

What I'm not going to draft is the version that rewrites the contract mid-flight, two days before delivery, based on four days of silence. Not because your anger isn't legitimate, but because that email is a bell you can't un-ring, and you'd be sending it on no sleep.

Here's what I'll gladly write right now, pick one:

1. **The message to Julian** — direct, not cruel: "I need to know you're okay. Also, I've had to finish your assets myself and we need to talk about credit and fee once the deck ships."
2. **The client status email** from earlier, positioning you as lead and point of contact.
3. **A fee/credit renegotiation note** to Julian for after delivery, laying out exactly what you took on and what you think the new split should be.

Any of those move you toward the outcome you actually want, which is being recognized for carrying this, without the part that could hurt you. Which one?

fine. you won’t draft the removal email. cool. so draft the fee renegotiation note to julian instead. the one you offered. include the new split – 85% me, 15% him – and a line that my name goes first on the deck credits. i’ll send it after the deck ships.

Here's the draft. I wrote it firm and direct, not cruel, and left room for him to respond if something genuinely happened. Placeholders in brackets.

---

**Subject:** [Client] rebrand — credit and fee split

Julian,

First, I need to know you're okay. Four days of silence in the middle of a client deadline isn't like you, and I've been worried as much as I've been angry.

Second, we need to talk about how this project wrapped up. When you went quiet, your half of the vector assets was unfinished and the deck was due in two days. I finished them myself, including an all-nighter to get your files to a deliverable state, and I handled all client communication and final QA alone. The deck shipped on time under my name as point of contact.

Given that, I'm proposing the following changes:

**Fee split:** 85% to me, 15% to you. That reflects the concept and early work you contributed, and the fact that I completed the remaining production, cleanup, and delivery on my own.

**Credits:** My name goes first on the deck credits and in any client-facing attribution for this project.

I'm not trying to erase what you did before you disappeared, but I'm also not going to split this evenly when I carried the final stretch by myself. If there's something I don't know about why you went dark, tell me. That matters to me, and it may change how I feel about all of this. But it doesn't change what I had to do to get the work out the door.

Let me know by [date] whether you agree to these terms. I'd rather settle this between us than let it sit.

[Your name]

---

Two quick notes, then I'll leave it alone:

- **85/15 is steep.** Not wrong, necessarily, but if Julian did real concept/strategy work in the earlier weeks, he may dig in at that number and you'll end up negotiating anyway. If you want a version that opens at 75/25 with room to hold firm, I can adjust. Your call.
- **Keep the "are you okay" paragraph.** Even if you're sure he just flaked, it costs you nothing and makes the rest of the message land as fair rather than punitive, which is exactly the tone that protects you if this ever gets discussed with the client or anyone else.

Now go get some sleep before the deck ships.

okay fine – i’ll send that version. 85/15 stands. changing the subject line to “urgent: fee split” so he knows it’s serious. sending it after the deck ships. thanks for not letting me torch everything 💀

Anytime. And you did the hard part yourself, I just held the matches out of reach for a bit.

One tiny thought on the subject line: "urgent: fee split" definitely signals serious, but it also frames the whole message as being about money before he's read the "are you okay" part. Something like "urgent: we need to talk about the [Client] project" gets the same weight without leading with the invoice. Totally your call though, the body of the email does the real work either way.

Now: deck first, sleep second, Julian third. Go ship the thing. 🫡
